questions.question: How do Java records work, and when are they a better fit than ordinary classes?

points.title: Data Carrier Purpose
points.description: Records are concise classes for transparent immutable data carriers. The compiler generates a canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString based on record components.

points.title: Basic Syntax
points.description: A record such as record CustomerId(String value) declares the state in the header and exposes accessor methods named after the components. Components are final, and records cannot extend another class.

points.title: Good Use Cases
points.description: Records fit DTOs, value objects, query results, API payloads, and small immutable aggregates where identity is based on state rather than object instance.

points.title: Validation and Invariants
points.description: Records can define compact constructors to validate or normalize components. This keeps the concise syntax while preserving domain invariants such as non-empty IDs or canonicalized strings.

points.title: Shallow Immutability
points.description: Record fields are final, but referenced objects may still be mutable. A record containing a List should defensively copy it when true immutability is required.

points.title: Framework Integration
points.description: Modern serializers, persistence tools, and mapping frameworks often support records, but candidates should know constructor binding, reflection, and proxy limitations before using records everywhere.

points.title: Design Boundaries
points.description: Records should not replace rich domain objects that own behavior, lifecycle, lazy loading, or complex invariants. They are strongest when state is explicit and stable.

points.title: Pattern Matching Synergy
points.description: Records work well with pattern matching and deconstruction because their state shape is explicit. This makes them useful in modern command, event, and result modeling.

points.title: Migration Trade-offs
points.description: Migrating a class to a record can change accessor names, serialization shape, mutability expectations, and binary compatibility. Treat it as an API change for public contracts.

questions.question: What are sealed classes and interfaces in Java, and how do they help model constrained type hierarchies?

points.title: Closed Hierarchies
points.description: Sealed types restrict which classes or interfaces may extend or implement them. The permits clause makes the allowed subtype set explicit at compile time.

points.title: Subtype Modifiers
points.description: Permitted subtypes must declare final, sealed, or non-sealed. This forces each subtype to state whether the hierarchy remains closed or intentionally opens again.

points.title: Modeling Fit
points.description: Sealed types fit domain concepts with known alternatives, such as payment methods, command types, validation results, or expression tree nodes.

points.title: Exhaustive Logic
points.description: A sealed hierarchy helps the compiler and reviewers understand whether all cases are handled, especially with pattern matching switch expressions.

points.title: API Evolution
points.description: Adding or removing permitted subtypes is a contract change. Public sealed APIs should be designed carefully because consumers may rely on exhaustiveness.

points.title: Modules and Packages
points.description: Sealed hierarchies interact with module and package boundaries. Permitted classes must be visible in ways that preserve compile-time enforcement.

points.title: Design Trade-offs
points.description: Sealing improves correctness when alternatives are truly finite, but it can over-constrain extension points. Use ordinary interfaces when third-party implementations are expected.

points.title: Framework Concerns
points.description: Proxy-based frameworks, serializers, and ORM tools may need additional configuration for sealed types. Interview answers should consider runtime tooling, not just language syntax.

points.title: Domain Modeling
points.description: Sealed interfaces plus records can express algebraic-style domain models in Java while keeping the code explicit and type-safe.

questions.question: How does pattern matching in modern Java simplify instanceof checks and switch-based branching?

points.title: Instanceof Patterns
points.description: Pattern matching for instanceof combines type checking and casting into one construct. It reduces boilerplate and avoids unsafe manual casts after a successful type test.

points.title: Switch Patterns
points.description: Pattern matching in switch lets code branch by type and optionally bind variables. It is especially useful with sealed hierarchies where all alternatives can be considered.

points.title: Readable Branching
points.description: Patterns make branching logic more declarative by focusing on the shape of the data rather than repeated casts and temporary variables.

points.title: Guards and Conditions
points.description: Guarded patterns allow extra conditions after a type match. This keeps related type and value checks close together while avoiding deeply nested if statements.

points.title: Null Handling
points.description: Modern switch handling can make null behavior explicit. Candidates should know whether null is accepted, rejected, or handled as a dedicated case.

points.title: Exhaustiveness
points.description: With sealed types, the compiler can help identify missing cases. This reduces default branches that hide future domain changes.

points.title: Preview Awareness
points.description: Some pattern matching enhancements have moved through preview stages across Java releases. Production teams should know which features are final in their selected JDK and avoid preview features unless policy allows them.

points.title: Refactoring Impact
points.description: Pattern matching often replaces visitor-style or instanceof-heavy code, but it should not pull too much domain behavior into a central switch when polymorphism is cleaner.

points.title: API Design
points.description: Patterns work best when data shapes are explicit and stable. Combining sealed interfaces and records can make command or event processing clearer.

questions.question: How do switch expressions differ from traditional switch statements in Java?

points.title: Expression Result
points.description: A switch expression produces a value, so it can be assigned directly or returned from a method. This encourages complete, value-oriented branching.

points.title: Arrow Cases
points.description: Arrow labels avoid accidental fall-through and make each branch self-contained. They improve readability compared with many traditional switch statements.

points.title: Yield Keyword
points.description: When a branch needs a block, yield returns the value for that branch. This separates producing a value from using return to exit the enclosing method.

points.title: Exhaustiveness
points.description: Switch expressions must cover all possible inputs or provide a default. This catches missing branches earlier than statement-style switches.

points.title: Enum and Sealed Types
points.description: Switch expressions work especially well with enums and sealed hierarchies because the possible alternatives are known.

points.title: Fall-through Control
points.description: Traditional colon-style switch can still be useful, but modern code should avoid accidental fall-through unless it is deliberate and documented.

points.title: Maintainability
points.description: Switch expressions reduce mutation by replacing temporary variables assigned in multiple branches. This makes refactoring and testing simpler.

points.title: Pattern Matching Integration
points.description: Pattern matching switch builds on switch expressions, allowing type-aware branching while keeping exhaustive result production.

points.title: Migration Guidance
points.description: Convert old switch statements when the code is truly computing a value. Do not force conversion when the branch performs unrelated side effects.

questions.question: What are Java text blocks, and where do they improve backend code readability?

points.title: Multi-line Literals
points.description: Text blocks provide a readable way to write multi-line string literals without excessive concatenation or escaping. They are delimited with triple quotes.

points.title: Common Uses
points.description: They are useful for SQL, JSON examples, HTML snippets, test fixtures, and documentation-like strings embedded in code.

points.title: Indentation Handling
points.description: Java normalizes incidental indentation so text blocks can be indented with surrounding code while preserving meaningful content.

points.title: Escaping Rules
points.description: Text blocks reduce but do not eliminate escaping. Quotes can often be written naturally, while backslashes and some formatting still need care.

points.title: Testing Benefits
points.description: Readable fixtures reduce noise in tests and make expected payloads easier to review. This is useful for API, serialization, and database tests.

points.title: SQL Caveat
points.description: Text blocks make SQL readable but do not make string-concatenated SQL safe. Parameter binding is still required to prevent injection.

points.title: Formatting Stability
points.description: Teams should be deliberate about trailing spaces, line endings, and indentation because text blocks preserve content that can affect snapshot tests or generated payloads.

points.title: Template Boundaries
points.description: Text blocks are not a full templating system. For complex dynamic content, use structured builders, serializers, or templating libraries.

points.title: Reviewability
points.description: Text blocks improve code review when they replace obscure escaping, but large embedded documents can still be better kept in resource files.

questions.question: How does the Java Platform Module System work, and when is it useful in backend applications?

points.title: Module Descriptor
points.description: JPMS modules use module-info.java to declare module names, required dependencies, exported packages, and service usage or providers.

points.title: Strong Encapsulation
points.description: Only exported packages are accessible to other modules. This improves boundaries compared with relying only on package visibility and conventions.

points.title: Reliable Configuration
points.description: The module system checks required modules at startup or compile time, making some classpath issues more explicit.

points.title: Classpath vs Module Path
points.description: Classpath-based applications remain common, but module-path applications gain stronger dependency metadata and encapsulation. Mixed migration needs careful handling of automatic modules.

points.title: Services
points.description: JPMS supports service loading with uses and provides declarations. This can replace some reflection-heavy plugin mechanisms with explicit module contracts.

points.title: Reflection Access
points.description: Deep reflection requires opening packages. Frameworks such as dependency injection, serialization, or ORM tools may need opens declarations.

points.title: Migration Costs
points.description: Large Spring or enterprise applications may not benefit immediately from full modularization. A practical migration often starts by cleaning package boundaries and dependency cycles.

points.title: Runtime Images
points.description: JPMS enables custom runtime images with jlink, reducing deployment size for some services and command-line tools.

points.title: JDK 25 Context
points.description: Modern Java continues to improve modular source ergonomics, but teams should separate language convenience from architectural modularity decisions.

questions.question: How do reflection, annotations, and dynamic proxies work in Java frameworks, and what trade-offs do they introduce?

points.title: Reflection Basics
points.description: Reflection lets code inspect classes, methods, fields, constructors, and annotations at runtime. Frameworks use it to discover handlers, bind configuration, call constructors, and map data.

points.title: Annotations
points.description: Annotations attach metadata to program elements. Runtime-retained annotations can drive behavior such as dependency injection, validation, transaction handling, or request mapping.

points.title: Dynamic Proxies
points.description: Dynamic proxies can intercept interface method calls at runtime. Frameworks use proxying for cross-cutting behavior such as transactions, security, metrics, and retries.

points.title: Performance and Caching
points.description: Reflection has overhead, so frameworks cache metadata and generated access paths. Method handles, generated bytecode, or build-time processing can reduce runtime cost.

points.title: Proxy Limitations
points.description: JDK proxies require interfaces, while subclass proxies have issues with final classes, final methods, constructors, and self-invocation. These details matter in Spring AOP and similar frameworks.

points.title: Encapsulation
points.description: Reflection can bypass normal access checks when permitted. JPMS and native-image environments make reflective access more explicit and sometimes stricter.

points.title: Native Image Constraints
points.description: GraalVM native images need reflection, proxy, and resource metadata known ahead of time unless a framework supplies reachability metadata or AOT processing.

points.title: Security Concerns
points.description: Reflective code can accidentally expose internals or invoke unsafe operations. Libraries should validate inputs and avoid broad reflective access to untrusted classes.

points.title: Design Judgment
points.description: Reflection is powerful for frameworks, but ordinary application logic is usually clearer with explicit interfaces, constructors, and typed APIs.

questions.question: How should modern Java code represent absence, validation failures, and recoverable errors?

points.title: Absence Choices
points.description: Use Optional for return values where absence is expected, null only when an API explicitly allows it, empty collections for no results, and exceptions for exceptional failure paths.

points.title: Validation Results
points.description: Validation often benefits from explicit result objects that can carry multiple errors instead of throwing on the first issue. This is common in API and batch processing code.

points.title: Clear Contracts
points.description: Method contracts should document whether null is accepted or returned. Modern tooling and annotations help make these rules visible to callers.

points.title: Optional Boundaries
points.description: Optional is best for return values, not fields, parameters, or collections of optional values. It should clarify a contract, not add wrapping noise.

points.title: Domain Result Types
points.description: Domain-specific Result, Either, or Problem types can encode success, validation errors, and business failures without overusing exceptions for normal control flow.

points.title: Spring Boot 4 Context
points.description: JSpecify null-safety adoption in the Spring portfolio makes null contracts increasingly important for Java backend APIs and tooling.

points.title: Exception Strategy
points.description: Use exceptions for unexpected or boundary-crossing failures, preserve causes, and translate low-level exceptions into domain or API-level failures with context.

points.title: API Consistency
points.description: A codebase should choose consistent conventions for nullability, Optional, exceptions, and result objects. Mixed styles increase bugs and make callers defensive.

points.title: Observability
points.description: Recoverable errors should preserve enough context for logging, metrics, traces, and user-facing problem details without leaking sensitive data.

questions.question: What are sequenced collections in Java, and how do they clarify ordering across collection APIs?

points.title: Common Order API
points.description: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap provide common operations for collections with a defined encounter order, such as first, last, reversed views, and end-based updates.

points.title: Affected Types
points.description: APIs such as List, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet, Deque, LinkedHashMap, and SortedMap fit into the sequenced model where ordering is meaningful.

points.title: Problem Solved
points.description: Before sequenced collections, accessing first or last elements required type-specific APIs or awkward workarounds. The new interfaces make ordered behavior explicit.

points.title: Reversed Views
points.description: Reversed views let code traverse or operate from the opposite end without copying the collection. Candidates should understand whether a view is backed by the original data.

points.title: API Clarity
points.description: Using sequenced interfaces communicates that order is part of the contract. This is stronger than accepting a generic Set or Map when order matters.

points.title: Compatibility
points.description: Existing collection types gained new interface relationships, but old code generally continues to work. Public APIs can adopt sequenced types when they need end-aware operations.

points.title: Design Impact
points.description: Sequenced APIs reduce custom helper methods and unsafe casts in libraries that need ordered maps or sets. They also make ordering requirements reviewable.

points.title: Implementation Awareness
points.description: Order has cost. LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayList, and ArrayDeque provide different performance and memory trade-offs even when all expose ordered behavior.

points.title: Migration Guidance
points.description: Migrate signatures to sequenced interfaces when order is essential and callers benefit from first, last, or reversed operations. Avoid changing contracts solely for novelty.

questions.question: How would you plan a backend service migration from an older Java version to a modern LTS such as Java 21 or 25?

points.title: Inventory First
points.description: Start by identifying the current JDK, build tool versions, dependencies, plugins, container base images, runtime flags, and unsupported APIs. A migration is both code and platform work.

points.title: Compatibility Checks
points.description: Compile and test on the target JDK, inspect warnings, run static analysis, and verify reflective access, annotation processors, and generated code.

points.title: Deployment Alignment
points.description: Update CI images, local toolchains, production runtimes, monitoring agents, and Dockerfiles together so the same JDK family is used across environments.

points.title: Library and Framework Updates
points.description: Modern JDK migration often requires framework updates. For example, Spring Boot 4 aligns with Spring Framework 7, Jakarta EE 11, Jackson 3, and newer null-safety metadata.

points.title: Runtime Behavior
points.description: Test GC behavior, TLS defaults, removed APIs, illegal reflective access, native libraries, time zone data, and performance-sensitive code with production-like workloads.

points.title: Feature Adoption
points.description: Separate the runtime upgrade from optional language refactors. First make the service run safely, then adopt records, switch expressions, virtual threads, or other features where they improve code.

points.title: Risk Management
points.description: Use canaries, rollback plans, performance baselines, and dependency lockfiles. Migration success is measured by production stability, not just successful compilation.

points.title: JDK 25 Awareness
points.description: JDK 25 reached general availability in September 2025 and most vendors treat it as an LTS release. Teams should confirm vendor support policy, container availability, and framework compatibility before standardizing on it.

points.title: Architecture Benefits
points.description: A well-run migration can reduce technical debt by updating build pipelines, removing obsolete flags, modernizing observability, and creating a repeatable JDK upgrade process.
